title: How does multi-level caching (L1 local in-memory like Caffeine in front of L2 Redis) absorb a stampede burst — when Redis expires a key, each instance briefly serves it from L1 so only one request per instance reloads — and what is the consistency trade-off (short L1 TTL = less stale, longer L1 TTL = stronger DB protection)?
shortTitle: How does multi-level caching absorb a stampede burst?

s1_definition.profdef: Multi-level caching layers a small, fast, per-process in-memory cache (level one, typically Caffeine) in front of a shared distributed cache (level two, typically Redis), which itself sits in front of the database. A read checks level one first, then level two on a miss, then the database on a level-two miss, populating the upper layers on the way back. This absorbs a stampede burst because when a key expires in the shared level-two cache, each application instance still briefly has the value in its own level-one cache, so within a short window only one request per instance (not per request) falls through to reload, dramatically cutting the number of reloads that reach level two and the database. The consistency trade-off is governed by the level-one time-to-live: a short level-one time-to-live means entries are less stale because each instance re-checks level two sooner, while a longer level-one time-to-live gives stronger protection to the database because instances serve from level one for longer and fall through less often, at the cost of more staleness.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, imagine the authoritative rate book is in the vault (the database), a shared whiteboard in the central hall holds the current rate for all tellers (Redis, level two), and each teller also keeps a quick sticky note of it at their own window (Caffeine, level one). When a customer asks, the teller glances at their sticky note first, then the hall whiteboard, then sends someone to the vault only if both are blank. Now suppose the hall whiteboard gets wiped at noon (the shared key expires). Without the sticky notes, every teller for every customer would rush to the vault at once — a stampede. But because each teller still has their own sticky note for a little while, each window only sends one runner to refresh, not one per customer, so the vault sees a handful of runners instead of a mob. How long the sticky note stays valid is the trade-off: a short note life means tellers re-check the whiteboard often so figures are fresh, while a long note life means the vault is bothered far less but the figure on the note can be a bit out of date.
s1_definition.oneliner: Multi-level caching puts a per-process Caffeine level one in front of a shared Redis level two, so when a level-two key expires each instance keeps serving from its own level one and only one request per instance reloads instead of one per request, and the level-one time-to-live tunes the trade-off between freshness (short) and database protection (long).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Multi-level caching layers a small, fast, per-process in-memory cache (level one, typically Caffeine) in front of a shared distributed cache (level two, typically Redis), which itself sits in front of the database. A read checks level one first, then level two on a miss, then the database on a level-two miss, populating the upper layers on the way back. This absorbs a stampede burst because when a key expires in the shared level-two cache, each application instance still briefly has the value in its own level-one cache, so within a short window only one request per instance (not per request) falls through to reload, dramatically cutting the number of reloads that reach level two and the database. The consistency trade-off is governed by the level-one time-to-live: a short level-one time-to-live means entries are less stale because each instance re-checks level two sooner, while a longer level-one time-to-live gives stronger protection to the database because instances serve from level one for longer and fall through less often, at the cost of more staleness.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, imagine the authoritative rate book is in the vault (the database), a shared whiteboard in the central hall holds the current rate for all tellers (Redis, level two), and each teller also keeps a quick sticky note of it at their own window (Caffeine, level one). When a customer asks, the teller glances at their sticky note first, then the hall whiteboard, then sends someone to the vault only if both are blank. Now suppose the hall whiteboard gets wiped at noon (the shared key expires). Without the sticky notes, every teller for every customer would rush to the vault at once — a stampede. But because each teller still has their own sticky note for a little while, each window only sends one runner to refresh, not one per customer, so the vault sees a handful of runners instead of a mob. How long the sticky note stays valid is the trade-off: a short note life means tellers re-check the whiteboard often so figures are fresh, while a long note life means the vault is bothered far less but the figure on the note can be a bit out of date.

**One line to remember:** Multi-level caching puts a per-process Caffeine level one in front of a shared Redis level two, so when a level-two key expires each instance keeps serving from its own level one and only one request per instance reloads instead of one per request, and the level-one time-to-live tunes the trade-off between freshness (short) and database protection (long).

sections.s2_technical:
The structure is a hierarchy of caches ordered by speed and scope. Level one is an in-process cache like Caffeine, which is the fastest because a lookup is a method call against a concurrent map in the same JVM with no network hop, but its scope is a single instance, so every instance has its own independent level one. Level two is a shared distributed cache like Redis, which every instance reads and writes over the network, so it is slower than level one (hundreds of microseconds versus nanoseconds) but shared across all instances. Behind both is the database, the slow source of truth. A read flows level one, then level two, then database, and populates upward: a database read fills level two and level one, a level-two hit fills level one. This is a layered cache-aside arrangement.

The reason this absorbs stampedes is best seen by comparing it to a single shared cache. With only Redis, when a hot key expires, the next read from every instance misses Redis and falls through to the database, and because the key is hot, many concurrent requests across all instances hit the database simultaneously — a stampede. The database is overwhelmed by a synchronized flood for one key precisely when the cache was supposed to protect it. The level-one cache breaks this synchronization at the instance boundary. When the Redis key expires, each instance's level one may still hold the value (because level-one entries have their own time-to-live independent of Redis), so reads continue to be served from level one without touching Redis or the database at all. Only when an instance's level-one entry also expires does that instance fall through, and even then you want only one request from that instance to reload while the rest wait or get the stale value. The net effect is that the number of reloads reaching the lower layers drops from "one per concurrent request" to roughly "one per instance per level-one time-to-live window," which for a fleet of a few dozen instances with a short window is orders of magnitude fewer.

To make the per-instance behavior truly one reload rather than a mini-stampede inside each instance, you combine level one with single-flight semantics. Caffeine's loading cache already provides this: when many threads in one instance miss the same key, only one thread performs the load and the others wait for its result, so each instance issues at most one reload to level two or the database per key. Layering single-flight at both levels — one reload per instance at level one, and ideally a lock or single-flight at level two so that the handful of instances that do fall through do not all hit the database — compounds the protection, so the database might see just one reload for a hot key even across the whole fleet.

The consistency trade-off is entirely about the level-one time-to-live, and it is a genuine tension with no free lunch. Because level one is per-instance and not invalidated when another instance writes, a value cached in level one can be stale for up to its time-to-live even after the underlying data changed and even after Redis was updated. A short level-one time-to-live (say one or two seconds) minimizes this staleness because each instance re-checks Redis frequently and picks up changes quickly, but it also means instances fall through to Redis more often, so the stampede protection is weaker and Redis sees more load. A long level-one time-to-live (say thirty seconds) makes instances serve from level one for much longer, so Redis and the database are bothered far less and stampede protection is strong, but a change can take up to thirty seconds to become visible on an instance, which is more staleness. You choose the level-one time-to-live based on how much staleness the data tolerates: a displayed aggregate can take a few seconds of staleness for strong protection, while data that must be near-real-time gets a very short level-one time-to-live or is not level-one-cached at all.

Invalidation across instances is the hard part of multi-level caching, because writing to Redis does not clear the stale copies sitting in every instance's level one. For data where the short time-to-live is acceptable, you simply let the level-one entries expire, accepting the bounded staleness. For data where you need prompt invalidation, you add a broadcast mechanism: when a value changes, you publish an invalidation message (for example via Redis publish/subscribe or a message topic) that every instance subscribes to, and on receiving it each instance evicts that key from its level one. This gives near-immediate cross-instance invalidation at the cost of extra machinery and the small window between the write and the broadcast arriving. The choice between time-to-live-based and broadcast-based invalidation is itself a trade-off between simplicity and freshness.

A senior nuance is that multi-level caching shines specifically for hot keys read far more than written, where the staleness of a short level-one time-to-live is acceptable and the read volume is high enough that the extra layer pays off; for cold or rarely-read keys the level one adds little. Another nuance is memory: level one must be bounded (a maximum size with an eviction policy like size-based LRU) so it does not consume unbounded heap in each instance, which is why Caffeine's size and time eviction are configured deliberately. A final nuance is that the layers can use different patterns — level one as refresh-ahead to avoid blocking, level two as cache-aside with a lock for single-flight — and the overall design is about placing the right protection at each layer so that a burst is progressively filtered: level one absorbs most of it per instance, level two absorbs most of what gets through across instances, and the database sees only a trickle.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India serves a hot computed interest rate across many instances, and a single shared cache was stampeding the database on expiry.

Problem 1 — With only Redis, when the rate key expired, every instance for every concurrent request missed and hit the database at once, overwhelming it. The team added a per-instance Caffeine level one in front of Redis. This is the multi-level structure.

Problem 2 — After adding level one, when the Redis key expired, each instance kept serving the rate from its own level one for a short window, so only one request per instance fell through to reload instead of one per request. This is the stampede absorption.

Problem 3 — The team had to choose the level-one time-to-live: a short one kept the displayed rate fresh but let more load through, a longer one protected the database more but allowed more staleness. They picked a short level-one time-to-live for freshness plus a publish/subscribe invalidation broadcast for prompt cross-instance eviction on rate changes. This is the consistency trade-off and invalidation.

We will model two application instances, each with a Caffeine-style level one in front of a shared Redis-style level two in front of a database, simulate a level-two expiry under a burst, and count how many reloads reach level two and the database with and without level one, then show the level-one time-to-live trade-off and a broadcast invalidation.

The code will have a `Database`, a shared `L2Cache`, a per-instance `L1Cache` with single-flight, an `AppInstance` that reads through the layers, and a demo running a burst across two instances and measuring reload counts.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a hot savings interest rate, two application instances each with a two-second level-one cache sharing one level-two cache in front of the database, and a burst of reads.

Step 1 — Both instances are warmed, so each has the rate in its own level one and the shared level two holds it too. The database read counters are reset so we can measure reloads.

Step 2 — The level-two key expires, and a burst of twenty requests per instance arrives while the level-one entries are still within their two-second life. Every one of those requests is served from the instance's own level one, so none of them touch level two or the database. The level-one caches absorbed the entire burst, and the database is barely touched.

Step 3 — The demo reports that during the burst the number of level-two reloads and database reads is essentially zero, demonstrating that the per-instance level one shielded both lower layers from the synchronized flood that a single shared cache would have suffered.

Step 4 — Time advances past the two-second level-one life, so now the level-one entries are stale and the next burst falls through. But because each instance uses single-flight, only one request per instance actually reloads while the others wait for it, so the level two sees about one reload per instance — roughly two across the fleet — rather than one per request. This is the key number: reloads scale with the number of instances, not the number of requests.

Step 5 — Finally, the rate is changed in the database, and an invalidation broadcast is delivered to both instances, each of which evicts the key from its level one. When instance two reads again, its level one is empty, so it fetches the updated rate promptly rather than waiting up to the full level-one life for the stale copy to expire. This shows the consistency mechanism that complements the short time-to-live.

```
2026-10-24 17:43:30 [INFO] === L2 expired; burst across 2 instances — L1 absorbs it ===
2026-10-24 17:43:30 [INFO] During burst within L1 TTL: L2 reloads=0, DB reads=0 (served from L1, DB barely touched)
2026-10-24 17:43:30 [INFO] === L1 TTL elapsed; each instance reloads ONCE (single-flight) ===
2026-10-24 17:43:30 [INFO] After L1 TTL: L2 reloads=1 (≈ one per instance), NOT one per request
2026-10-24 17:43:30 [INFO] === Rate change → broadcast invalidation evicts L1 on all instances ===
2026-10-24 17:43:30 [INFO] inst-2 sees new rate promptly: 400
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Multi-level caching layers a small, fast, per-process in-memory cache like Caffeine as level one in front of a shared distributed cache like Redis as level two, which itself sits in front of the database. A read checks level one, then level two on a miss, then the database, populating the upper layers on the way back. Level one is fastest because it is an in-JVM method call with no network hop, but its scope is one instance, so every instance has its own; level two is shared across all instances but slower because it is a network call.

This absorbs a stampede burst by breaking the synchronization at the instance boundary. With only Redis, when a hot key expires, the next read from every instance for every concurrent request misses and hits the database at once, a synchronized flood that overwhelms the database precisely when the cache should protect it. With a per-instance level one, when the Redis key expires each instance may still hold the value in its own level one, so reads keep being served from level one without touching Redis or the database. Only when an instance's level-one entry also expires does that instance fall through, and with single-flight only one request per instance reloads while the rest wait or get the current value. So the number of reloads reaching the lower layers drops from one per request to roughly one per instance per level-one window, which across a fleet is orders of magnitude fewer, and layering single-flight at level two as well means the database might see just one reload for a hot key across the whole fleet.

The consistency trade-off is entirely about the level-one time-to-live, and it is a real tension. Because level one is per-instance and is not invalidated when another instance writes, a value in level one can be stale for up to its time-to-live even after Redis and the database were updated. A short level-one time-to-live minimizes staleness because each instance re-checks Redis sooner, but it weakens stampede protection because instances fall through more often; a long level-one time-to-live gives strong protection because instances serve from level one longer, but allows more staleness. I choose it by how much staleness the data tolerates, and where I need prompt cross-instance freshness I add a broadcast invalidation over Redis publish/subscribe so that on a write every instance evicts the key from its level one, rather than waiting for the time-to-live to lapse.

In my banking work I used this for a hot computed interest rate served across many instances, where a single shared Redis cache was stampeding the database on expiry. Adding a short-lived Caffeine level one meant that when the Redis key expired each instance kept serving from its level one and only one request per instance fell through, so the database saw a trickle instead of a flood, and I paired the short level-one time-to-live with a publish/subscribe invalidation broadcast so a rate change became visible promptly instead of lingering for the full level-one window.

The nuances I always add are that multi-level caching shines for hot keys read far more than written where a couple of seconds of staleness is acceptable, that level one must be bounded with a size and eviction policy so it does not consume unbounded heap per instance, and that the layers can run different patterns — level one as refresh-ahead to never block, level two as cache-aside with single-flight — so a burst is progressively filtered: level one absorbs most of it per instance, level two absorbs most of what gets through, and the database sees almost none.
